Zig needed a std.posix.getenv→std.c.getenv fix (0.16) before it would build. `thru*` = throughput over a **fixed** input pair (Go, Rust, Swift, Zig harnesses — best-case, branch-predicted; mutually comparable). `thru‡` = the JVM (Java, Kotlin) fixed-operand harness; **measured verify-off (production)**. The JVM ports allocate a result object per op (value-type ports don't). Whether that shows up depends on the harness AND on whether C2 elides it — and the two JVM ports behave **differently**: - **Java**: consuming the result via `d128_ubdLo64(op(a,b))` let C2 Escape Analysis scalar-replace the object (allocation genuinely vanished, add-SQ 0.77 ns). **Run `e2`** forces escape (store into a heap array) ⇒ the 32 B/op reappears (add-SQ 3.48). - **Kotlin**: **run `Rko2` measured this directly** with `getThreadAllocatedBytes` and found the result is **NOT scalar-replaced** — the elided and escaped kernels allocate the *same* bytes/op (add-SQ 32, div 192–248). So Kotlin's escape guard changes **dead-vs-live** (barrier + GC), not alloc-vs-none; the object is allocated either way (likely the FNZ/ finalize-heavy path exceeds C2's inline budget so the `new` stays in a non-inlined callee). The earlier "Kotlin EA-elided" claim was an unverified assumption, now falsified. Both JVM ports' honest alloc-inclusive add-SQ is ~3.3–3.5 ns; the value-type ports pay **zero** allocation unconditionally. Verify config also matters (run `e`). Plain `thru` = the C swept 4096-input dataset (average-case). Absolute ns/op still carry small per-harness floors (Swift's black-box tax is the largest, ~0.5-1 ns); the **ratio vs each alternative is the reliable cross-cutting number**. **Cross-port fairness — a recorded ns/op is `engine + packaging`, and the packaging term differs by language.** Two per-harness costs ride on top of the (identical) decimal128 algorithm and must be discounted before reading a cross-port *absolute*: 1. **Black-box cost.** Zig `doNotOptimizeAway` and Rust `black_box` are free compiler barriers; Swift has none, so its harness routes an operand through an `@inline(never)` `opaque()` — a real call every iteration (~0.5–1 ns, the largest floor, irreducible without a better Swift black-box). 2. **Cross-module inlining.** Zig compiles the library from source into the bench (no ABI boundary ⇒ free inlining). Swift links a separately-compiled module, so **until run `Rsw2` the public `_tte` operators were real cross-module calls** — which inflated the Swift light bands (add/sub SQ/NQ/FQ, div PT) by **≈⅓ purely from packaging, not the engine**: NQ 6.20 vs the true 3.71, OQ 14.08 vs 10.28, PT1 7.34 vs 5.58. **`Rsw2` (CMO persisted in `Package.swift`) removes this**; the arithmetic-bound heavy bands (mul XP, div XD) barely moved, confirming it was call overhead. **Any earlier cross-port table using the pre-CMO Swift rows (run d/Rsw) understated Swift's engine on the light bands — use the `Rsw2` rows for cross-port comparison.** This packaging axis has NOT been audited identically for every port (Rust/Go benches are separate compilation units too; Go's gap is instead an engine-level non-LLVM-backend cost that survives any such fix) — see §7. Engine-level differences survive discounting the packaging term; packaging ones do not. ## 7. Open Items - ~~**C wide multiply (`mul XP`) is ~2× the LLVM cluster — optimization lead (run `Rcf`, §4.2).**~~ **DONE (same session).** The C fixed-operand arm measured `mul XP` at 40.49 ns vs rust 17.1 / zig 19.4 / swift 20.8 (matching C's own swept XP 36.6 — real, not a harness artifact). One line. **Result: mul XP 40.49 → 17.30 ns (2.36×), = rust; ctest 121/0** (all IBM fptest/rosetta vectors pass — correctness-neutral). This was C-only; rust/swift already route q128res in finalize and zig fixed its copy in `Rzg2`. (The Rsw3/`Rfma` "c/rust/swift already routed q128res in finalize" claim held for the FMA/add finalize path but NOT the mul-XP path.) - ~~**Kotlin (run `f`) is EA-elided — re-measure with the escape guard.**~~ **DONE** (run `Rko2`, §4/§6): added the escape guard (store results into a static heap array) AND a `getThreadAllocatedBytes` probe to `BenchTest.kt`. **Result overturned the premise:** Kotlin is **NOT scalar-replaced** — elided and escaped kernels allocate the same bytes/op (add-SQ 32, div 192–248), so the result is allocated either way. It *refuted* the run-j2 guess: generic CD (41 ns) ≈ ET (40), so the compact-divide weakness is the small-divisor 128÷64 kernel itself, not the terminating strip. New actionable findings instead ↓. - ~~**d128 lacks a general exact-divide early-out**~~ **DONE** (runs h2→h4). Two early-outs now ship: **PT** (`divPow10Divisor`, run h3, §2.4.9): 17.6 → **3.25 ns**, libbid **3.59×** (was 0.62×); and **ET** (quotient-first divide, run h4, §2.4.10): **40.9 → 8.26 ns, libbid 0.27× → 1.33×** — the exact case (`R0==0`) now terminates with no rounding and no strip.
